```{r, include = FALSE}
# the full examples run when the package is built; CRAN checks skip them for time
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = identical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"), "true"), collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
```

```{r setup}
library(bayescompR)
# chains run in parallel on this many cores; on your own machine use
# options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
options(mc.cores = 2)
```

MCMC estimates are only trustworthy when the chains have mixed. bayescompR
computes the diagnostics recommended by Vehtari et al. (2021), with results
identical to the posterior package, and the sampler diagnostics of Stan.

## R-hat and effective sample size

`bayescomp_rhat()` is the maximum of the rank normalized split R-hat and
the folded split R-hat. Splitting each chain in half detects trends within
chains, rank normalization makes it robust to heavy tails, and folding
($|x - \text{median}|$) detects chains that differ in scale. Values below
1.01 indicate convergence.

`bayescomp_ess_bulk()` estimates the effective sample size of the rank
normalized draws, relevant for means and medians; `bayescomp_ess_tail()`
is the smaller of the effective sample sizes of the 5% and 95% quantile
indicators, relevant for intervals. Both use Geyer's initial monotone
sequence estimator. Aim for at least 100 per chain.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
good <- matrix(rnorm(4000), 1000, 4)
stuck <- good
stuck[, 4] <- stuck[, 4] + 2           # one chain in a different place
ar <- apply(good, 2, function(z) stats::filter(z, 0.95, method = "recursive"))
c(rhat_good = bayescomp_rhat(good), rhat_stuck = bayescomp_rhat(stuck))
c(ess_good = bayescomp_ess_bulk(good), ess_autocorrelated = bayescomp_ess_bulk(ar))
c(mcse_mean = bayescomp_mcse_mean(good), mcse_sd = bayescomp_mcse_sd(good))
bayescomp_ess_quantile(good, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
bayescomp_mcse_quantile(good, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
```

Inputs are iterations by chains matrices. `summary()` applies these to
every variable of a fit, including the Monte Carlo standard errors of the
mean and the standard deviation (`mcse_mean`, `mcse_sd`): report a
posterior mean only to the digits its MCSE supports.

## Sampler diagnostics

`bayescomp_diagnose()` reports three Hamiltonian Monte Carlo diagnostics:

* **Divergent transitions.** The leapfrog integrator became unstable, the
  energy error exceeded 1000, usually in regions of high curvature. Even a
  few divergences can mean that part of the posterior is not explored.
* **Maximum tree depth.** NUTS stopped doubling before the trajectory
  turned around. This is an efficiency warning, not a validity one.
* **E-BFMI.** The energy Bayesian fraction of missing information; values
  below 0.3 mean the momentum resampling explores the energy distribution
  poorly, often for heavy tailed posteriors.

The per draw values are in `fit$sampler_diagnostics`: `accept_stat__`,
`stepsize__`, `treedepth__`, `n_leapfrog__`, `divergent__` and
`energy__`. E-BFMI per chain can be computed from `energy__` directly:

```{r}
fit_ok <- bayescomp_sample(bayescomp_model("parameters { vector[3] z; } model { z ~ std_normal(); }"),
                           chains = 2, iter_warmup = 300, iter_sampling = 300, seed = 1, refresh = 0)
e <- fit_ok$sampler_diagnostics[, , "energy__"]
apply(e, 2, function(x) sum(diff(x)^2) / sum((x - mean(x))^2))   # E-BFMI per chain
table(fit_ok$sampler_diagnostics[, , "treedepth__"])
```

## Plots

`plot()` draws trace plots by default; `type = "density"` the marginal
densities by chain, `"rank"` rank histograms (each chain's histogram
should be flat when the chains mix), and `"ess_local"` and
`"ess_quantile"` the effective sample size of small intervals and of
quantiles, which show where in the distribution the draws are scarce.

```{r, fig.height = 3}
plot(fit_ok, "z[1]")
plot(fit_ok, "z[1]", type = "density")
plot(fit_ok, "z[1]", type = "rank")
plot(fit_ok, "z[1]", type = "ess_quantile")
```

## Divergences in a funnel

Neal's funnel is the classic example of a geometry that defeats HMC. The
centered parameterization has a narrow neck where the step size adapted
for the wide region is far too large:

```{r}
centered <- bayescomp_model("
parameters { real v; vector[5] x; }
model { v ~ normal(0, 3); x ~ normal(0, exp(v / 2)); }")
fit_c <- bayescomp_sample(centered, chains = 2, iter_warmup = 300, iter_sampling = 300,
                          seed = 4, refresh = 0)
bayescomp_diagnose(fit_c)
summary(fit_c, "v")
```

The divergences flag that the neck (large negative `v`) is not explored,
and the posterior of `v` is biased (the true distribution is normal with
mean 0 and sd 3). The non centered parameterization samples a standard
normal and scales it, removing the funnel:

```{r}
noncentered <- bayescomp_model("
parameters { real v; vector[5] x_raw; }
transformed parameters { vector[5] x = exp(v / 2) * x_raw; }
model { v ~ normal(0, 3); x_raw ~ std_normal(); }")
fit_n <- bayescomp_sample(noncentered, chains = 2, iter_warmup = 300, iter_sampling = 300,
                          seed = 4, refresh = 0)
bayescomp_diagnose(fit_n)
summary(fit_n, "v")
```

Where divergences are located can be seen by plotting them:

```{r}
d <- bayescomp_draws(fit_c, c("v", "x[1]"), format = "matrix")
div <- as.vector(fit_c$sampler_diagnostics[, , "divergent__"]) == 1
plot(d[, "x[1]"], d[, "v"], pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = ifelse(div, "red", "grey50"),
     xlab = "x[1]", ylab = "v", main = "Centered funnel (divergences in red)")
```

Each fit also records where the divergent trajectories failed: element
`divergences` of the fit has the chain, the iteration and the parameter
values at the last point of the trajectory before its energy error grew
too large. These points sit in the neck of the funnel, which is more
informative than the draws of the divergent iterations, since those are
taken from the whole trajectory:

```{r}
head(fit_c$divergences[, c("chain", "iteration", "v", "x[1]")])
summary(fit_c$divergences$v)
plot(d[, "x[1]"], d[, "v"], pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = "grey60", xlab = "x[1]", ylab = "v",
     main = "Where divergent trajectories failed")
points(fit_c$divergences[["x[1]"]], fit_c$divergences$v, pch = 16, col = "red")
```

## Rejected proposals

A proposal is rejected when the log density cannot be evaluated: a
domain error (a negative scale), a `reject()` statement or a non finite
value. Stan prints these as informational messages; bayescompR counts
them by chain and reason, and `bayescomp_diagnose()` lists them. A few
rejections in early warmup are harmless; many during sampling point to
missing constraints on parameters.

```{r}
m_rej <- bayescomp_model("
parameters { real mu; real s; }
model { mu ~ normal(0, 1); s ~ normal(1, 0.5); 0.5 ~ normal(mu, s); }")
fit_rej <- bayescomp_sample(m_rej, chains = 2, iter_warmup = 200, iter_sampling = 200,
                            seed = 1, refresh = 0)
fit_rej$rejections
```

Declaring `real<lower=0> s;` removes them.

## What to change when a check fails

| Problem | First things to try |
|---|---|
| R-hat above 1.01 | run longer chains; look for multimodality with a trace or rank plot; reparameterize; try `bayescomp_smc()` or `bayescomp_parallel_tempering()` for several modes |
| Low bulk or tail ESS | run longer chains; `metric = "dense_e"` for correlated parameters; reparameterize |
| Divergent transitions | non centered parameterizations of hierarchical models; `adapt_delta = 0.95` or `0.99`; stronger priors on scale parameters |
| Maximum tree depth | `metric = "dense_e"`; rescale parameters to unit scale; raise `max_treedepth` |
| Low E-BFMI | reparameterize heavy tailed or funnel shaped parts |
| Many rejections | declare the constraints the parameters need (`<lower=0>` on scales) |

## Approximate methods

R-hat and ESS do not apply to Laplace, ADVI or Pathfinder draws, which are
independent draws from an approximation, and `bayescomp_diagnose()` says
so instead of reporting checks that cannot fail. Likewise tree depth is
checked only for NUTS, and divergences and E-BFMI only for NUTS and static
HMC. Their reliability is assessed
differently: Pathfinder reports the Pareto $\hat k$ of its importance
weights (`fit$pareto_k`, above 0.7 is unreliable), and the `log_p__` and
`log_g__` columns of Laplace and ADVI fits give the importance ratios for a
Pareto smoothed importance sampling check with the loo package:

```{r, eval = identical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"), "true") && requireNamespace("loo", quietly = TRUE)}
lap <- bayescomp_laplace(noncentered, draws = 1000, seed = 1)
log_ratio <- as.vector(bayescomp_draws(lap, "log_p__")) - as.vector(bayescomp_draws(lap, "log_g__"))
loo::psis(log_ratio, r_eff = NA)$diagnostics$pareto_k
```

A $\hat k$ above 0.7 means the approximation should not be used for
estimates, even by importance sampling. SMC reports
the temperatures and per stage Metropolis acceptance rates in
`fit$betas` and `fit$acceptance`.
